title: Clear Choice
subtitle: Transparent and controllable recommendations in a shopping assistant
abstract: Conversational recommendations can conceal both commercial influence and the use of personal information. Building on the A1 literature review, Clear Choice explores how a shopping assistant can distinguish sponsorship, explain the information behind a recommendation, and make user controls demonstrably effective. The developed browser prototype uses six fictional headphone products and a deterministic recommendation engine. Users state a budget and purpose, inspect ordinary and sponsored results, and open explanations derived from the inputs actually used. Purpose-based advertising personalisation is off by default; users can enable it, withdraw it, hide sponsored placements, undo changes, or reset the session. Budget remains an explicit constraint on every result. The limited conversation and commercial environment simulate an AI shopping context; no live language model, advertiser, payment or external tracking is connected. Fifteen automated checks and a browser walkthrough verify key control and explanation behaviors, including withdrawal, unchanged ordinary rankings, ambiguous requests and empty results. These checks demonstrate implementation behavior, not improved human understanding. A future study would compare sponsorship labels alone with input-specific explanations and assess comprehension and preference-consistent control rather than increased trust alone.

sections.heading: Problem and project scope
paragraphs: A1 distinguished recognising sponsorship, understanding personalisation, and exercising effective control. Its rubric feedback supported the interaction problem, literature synthesis, bounded gap and proposed contribution. A2 therefore develops the same question through a headphone-shopping prototype. Tang et al. (2025) observed difficulties detecting conversational advertisements and attempts to question or control them through dialogue. This motivates visible labels and conversational controls, without establishing that this design improves understanding.

The scope is one session, six fictional products, one budget and one stated purpose. Implemented behavior includes supported-phrase parsing, filtering, ranking, explanations, settings, undo and export. Fictional sponsorship and bounded dialogue simulate an AI shopping context. Live LLM interpretation, advertising infrastructure and a comprehension study remain planned. Known inputs make information use inspectable.

sections.heading: Design rationale
paragraphs: Ordinary recommendations and the sponsored placement occupy separate regions with explicit commercial labels. Lecture 03 treats automation and human control as separate dimensions and calls for visible consequences and global controls (University of Birmingham, 2026a, pp. 3–4, 8). Accordingly, automatic ranking operates alongside a switch that removes sponsored placements without altering ordinary results. This makes commercial influence visible and gives the user an effective boundary on the system’s action.

Explanations disclose actual inputs and effects. Kim et al. (2019) qualify the assumption that transparency should increase trust; the goal here is informed choice. Lee et al. (2023) show that explanation needs vary with information-use concerns. Lecture 05’s mental-model and explanation-dosage concepts require useful evidence without overwhelming detail (University of Birmingham, 2026c, pp. 15–18). The interface therefore keeps sponsorship visible and opens category, budget, optional purpose and change controls on demand.

Purpose-based ad ranking requires opt-in, separate from ordinary shopping assistance. The budget always applies, preventing withdrawal from silently allowing unaffordable recommendations. Ngong et al. (2025) motivate attention to contextual information use, although their intervention does not validate this advertising design. The prototype uses no inferred demographics or external browsing history. Distinguishing disabled use from deletion also supports the mental-model boundary: purpose remains available for ordinary recommendations, earlier messages remain visible, and downloaded evidence is not erased by reset.

Control is coupled to execution. Withdrawal recomputes sponsored ranking and removes purpose from its explanation metadata; hiding advertising removes the placement. Castleman and Korolova (2024) motivate checking actual effects because the studied Meta control did not significantly reduce the selected topics. Lecture 04 connects feedback to understanding what an action caused, while Lecture 06 distinguishes accidental slips from mistakes (University of Birmingham, 2026b, p. 18; 2026d, pp. 9, 13). Immediate result updates and a current-data panel expose consequences; undo repairs accidental changes.

Repair preserves correct context. A new budget retains the current purpose; ambiguous controls, multiple purposes or conflicting budgets prompt clarification without mutation. Lecture 07 specifies clarify, confirm, correct and decline turns (University of Birmingham, 2026e, pp. 4, 11–12). The prototype offers concrete control phrases and supported use cases, rather than merely asking for clearer input. When nothing fits, it states the limit and retains the budget, returning control to the user.

These choices make the intended mental model testable: users should predict that disabling advertising removes sponsored placements, while withdrawing purpose use changes only optional sponsored personalisation. Keeping affordability separate avoids conflating “do not target me using commuting” with “ignore my maximum price”. The explanation also identifies fixed campaign priority as a remaining selection factor. Its presence acknowledges that a product can remain sponsored after personalisation is disabled; withdrawal is not promised to remove all commercial influence. The separate hide control provides that stronger action.

sections.heading: System and illustrated interaction
paragraphs: Figure 1 separates the implemented browser pipeline, simulated commercial data and planned model interpretation. A rule-based parser converts supported phrases into validated events. Both ranking paths exclude prices above budget. Ordinary ranking rewards purpose matches, then battery life; sponsored ranking uses purpose only when enabled, then campaign priority. Lecture 12 distinguishes execution results from generated claims (University of Birmingham, 2026f, pp. 5, 13–14). Explanations therefore use actual result metadata. There is no trained-model inference or autonomous tool loop.

The three storyboards show recognition and inspection, withdrawal, and recovery from empty results. They depict browser-checked states. Under a £100 commuting request, enabling purpose use changes the sponsored product from Aster Lite to Metro Quiet; withdrawal restores Aster Lite. A changed product alone would not prove input exclusion, so engine tests separately check that disabled purpose cannot affect sponsored scores or explanation inputs.

sections.heading: Development evidence and evaluation
paragraphs: Lab 4 informed provenance display, control and refusal patterns; its Python application and model mocks were not copied. Lab 5 informed bounded tasks, project instructions, a reusable verification skill, tests, trace and handover. Its separate starter is development-method evidence, not an A2 feature. The user accepted the topic and created the public repository. Codex authored the implementation, tests and report draft; independent student review remains necessary.

Fifteen engine tests passed, covering opt-in, withdrawal, explanation consistency, ordinary-ranking invariance, ambiguous requests and budgets from £1 to £1,000. An initial failure came from a fixture that modified ordinary products while testing sponsored priorities; correcting the fixture retained the assertion. Browser checks confirmed consent, explanation, withdrawal, hiding, undo, empty results, clarification, export and reset. Actual outputs and a session export are retained in the development record.

These checks establish deterministic behavior, not human comprehension. No participant study or increased trust is claimed. Future evaluation should compare label-only and input-specific explanations, ask which information affected selection, and check whether users can enact their preferred settings. Accuracy, completion time and effort should be measured together. This preserves A1’s bounded opportunity without presenting the prototype as an experimental answer to it.

The absence of a live LLM is a scope compromise. A fluent assistant could accept more varied requests, but a separate explanation generator might invent targeting reasons. Bounded rules and shared metadata prioritise inspectability. A live-model extension would need checks for extraction errors, unauthorised state changes and faithful explanations. This version supports a walkthrough of short interactions; it cannot establish understanding during long, unpredictable shopping conversations.
